meta.title: Who really said "Outside of a dog, a book is man's best friend. Inside of a dog, it's too dark to read"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Groucho Marx. Quote Investigator traces the joke to newspaper columns from 1943 — originally about a horse. Groucho was only credited in 1973.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Outside of a dog, a book is man's best friend. Inside of a dog, it's too dark to read'?
meta.ogDescription: A thirty-year newspaper joke with no author. It began with a horse in 1943 and reached Groucho’s name in 1973, four years before he died.

answer.label: Not Groucho Marx — a newspaper joke with no known author
answer.authorDates: In print by July 1943 · originator never identified
answer.sourceLine: Nobody has ever established who wrote this. Quote Investigator ↗ follows it through American newspaper columns for thirty years before Groucho’s name appears, and the early versions are not even about a dog: the first instance QI has found, in The Chicago Daily News of 6 July 1943, is credited to a Chicago Board of Trade press officer named Francis Bisson and runs “Outside of a horse, man’s best friend is a book, but inside a horse it’s too dark to read.” QI’s verdict on the Marx attribution is that the evidence for it “is very weak”.

source.excerpt: Outside of a horse, man’s best friend is a book, but inside a horse it’s too dark to read.
trail: Quote Investigator’s article on the line ↗ lays out the chronology from primary newspaper citations. July 1943, The Chicago Daily News: the horse version credited to Francis Bisson. May 1947, the Nashville Banner: the horse version again, this time credited to the jockey Ted Atkinson ↗ — “probably because he is well-read and articulate”.

QI then tracks the joke mutating through columnists who were plainly just reworking a template. The dog arrives in December 1948, in the Binghamton Press — but with “policeman” swapped in for “book” — and a September 1950 instance opens the same way with “diamond”. The combination that makes the modern joke, a dog and a book and “too dark to read”, appears by November 1952 in The Nashville Tennessean, credited to a comic named Jimmy Husson. In February 1954 a form very close to the modern one ran in Boys’ Life’s reader-submitted joke column under the name of a boy in Cleveland.

The Groucho attribution arrives last. Per QI the earliest is a gossip column in the Philadelphia Daily News of 5 April 1973 — thirty years after the first citation, and in slightly different words: “Outside of a dog, a book is man’s best friend. That’s because inside a dog it’s too dark to read.” QI’s conclusion is that this “was a very late date” and the evidence for Marx “is very weak”.

Wikiquote ↗ files the line under Misattributed for Groucho and cites QI’s research for the same finding. Note that Wikiquote’s summary still names the May 1947 Ted Atkinson column as the first appearance; QI added the earlier July 1943 citation in an update dated 11 July 2026, which is the date used here.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest form Quote Investigator has located, from July 1943, and the animal is a horse. The switch to a dog is what makes the modern version work — it lets the first clause borrow the existing proverb about man’s best friend, so the joke sets its own trap. That refinement happened somewhere in a decade of anonymous newspaper reprinting, and no one knows who made it.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status is asserted, and none can honestly be. The wording has no identified author and no established first publication — it surfaces in a 1943 newspaper column already in circulation and is reworked by a dozen anonymous hands over the following decade. The individual newspapers and magazines that printed each variant are separate copyrighted works, cited here as evidence of the joke’s travels rather than as its origin.

author.metaLine: In print by July 1943 · from American newspaper humour columns
author.bio: No one has ever been identified as the author. The joke belongs to a vanished ecosystem: the daily newspaper humour column, where paragraphers swapped one-liners freely, credited them to whoever had said them last, and reworked them for a local angle. Quote Investigator has traced at least six different names attached to versions of this line between 1943 and 1975 — a press officer, a jockey, a nightclub comic, a Cleveland schoolboy, an obscure acquaintance of a sports columnist, and finally Groucho Marx. That pattern is the signature of a joke with no owner.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A library-poster favourite that six different people have been credited with, none of them convincingly.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the earliest Groucho attribution in a Philadelphia Daily News gossip column of 5 April 1973 — thirty years after the joke’s first documented appearance, and in different words. QI’s verdict: “the evidence supporting an ascription to Groucho is very weak.”

QI’s first citation, The Chicago Daily News of 6 July 1943, credits a horse version to Bisson, a public relations officer for the Chicago Board of Trade. Being the first name in print is not the same as being the author, and a column crediting a PR man with a gag is weak evidence either way.

Two 1947 columns pin the horse version on the jockey Ted Atkinson ↗, one of them explaining the choice as being “probably because he is well-read and articulate” — which is a columnist reasoning about who ought to have said it, not reporting that he did.

items.who: Jimmy Husson, Jim Brewer, Agro B. Arlo
items.why: QI records the joke credited to a nightclub comic in 1952, submitted by a boy in Cleveland to Boys’ Life in 1954, and attributed to an acquaintance of a sports columnist in 1975. A line that collects this many owners has none.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke was circulating in American newspapers by July 1943 ↗, about a horse, and no one has ever established who made it up. Groucho’s name was attached in 1973, last of at least six.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke’s evolution is easier to see than its author. The 1943 version is about a horse, which is nearly funny: the second clause lands, but the first has to explain itself. Swap in a dog and the sentence hijacks a proverb everyone already knows — man’s best friend — so the setup does no visible work and the punchline arrives from nowhere.

That improvement took about a decade of anonymous reprinting to arrive, and it is why the line is now on a thousand library walls. It also explains the drift to Groucho: by 1973 the joke sounded like a Groucho joke, because a decade of columnists had sanded it into one.
detailsBody: One caution about sources, since this page cites two. Wikiquote’s summary of the line still names the May 1947 Ted Atkinson column as its first appearance, because Quote Investigator only added the earlier July 1943 Chicago Daily News citation in an update dated 11 July 2026. Where the two disagree we have followed QI, which is the underlying research Wikiquote itself points to.
context.pull: It took ten years and a dozen anonymous columnists to turn a horse into a dog.
